    return $rev >> (32 - $k);
}

function modPow($a, $p) {
    $a = $a % MOD;
    if ($a < 0) $a += MOD;
    $result = 1;
    while ($p > 0) {
        if ($p % 2 == 1) {
            $result = ($result * $a) % MOD;
        }
        $a = ($a * $a) % MOD;
        $p = intdiv($p, 2);
    }
    return $result;
}

function modInv($a) {
    return modPow($a, MOD - 2);
}

function numberTheoreticTransform(&$coef, $k, $inverse) {
    $baseRoot = $inverse ? INVROOT : ROOT;
    $root = modPow($baseRoot, modPow(2, 23 - $k));
    $roots = array_fill(0, $k, 0);
    $roots[$k - 1] = $root;
    for ($i = $k - 1; $i > 0; $i--) {
        $roots[$i - 1] = ($roots[$i] * $roots[$i]) % MOD;
    }
    for ($s = 0; $s < $k; $s++) {
        $len = 1 << $s;
        for ($st = 0; $st < count($coef); $st += 2 * $len) {
            $curRoot = 1;
            for ($j = $st; $j < $st + $len; $j++) {
                $t = ($curRoot * $coef[$j + $len]) % MOD;
                $u = $coef[$j];

                $coef[$j + $len] = ($u - $t) % MOD;
                if ($coef[$j + $len] < 0) $coef[$j + $len] += MOD;
                $curRoot = ($roots[$s] * $curRoot) % MOD;
            }
        }
    }
}

source_data.prob_desc_description: All bus tickets in Berland have their numbers. A number consists of $$$n$$$ digits ($$$n$$$ is even). Only $$$k$$$ decimal digits $$$d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$$$ can be used to form ticket numbers. If $$$0$$$ is among these digits, then numbers may have leading zeroes. For example, if $$$n = 4$$$ and only digits $$$0$$$ and $$$4$$$ can be used, then $$$0000$$$, $$$4004$$$, $$$4440$$$ are valid ticket numbers, and $$$0002$$$, $$$00$$$, $$$44443$$$ are not.A ticket is lucky if the sum of first $$$n / 2$$$ digits is equal to the sum of remaining $$$n / 2$$$ digits. Calculate the number of different lucky tickets in Berland. Since the answer may be big, print it modulo $$$998244353$$$.
source_data.prob_desc_output_spec: Print the number of lucky ticket numbers, taken modulo $$$998244353$$$.
source_data.prob_desc_input_spec: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ $$$(2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5, 1 \le k \le 10)$$$ — the number of digits in each ticket number, and the number of different decimal digits that may be used. $$$n$$$ is even. The second line contains a sequence of pairwise distinct integers $$$d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$$$ $$$(0 \le d_i \le 9)$$$ — the digits that may be used in ticket numbers. The digits are given in arbitrary order.
source_data.prob_desc_notes: NoteIn the first example there are $$$6$$$ lucky ticket numbers: $$$1111$$$, $$$1818$$$, $$$1881$$$, $$$8118$$$, $$$8181$$$ and $$$8888$$$.There is only one ticket number in the second example, it consists of $$$20$$$ digits $$$6$$$. This ticket number is lucky, so the answer is $$$1$$$.
